lines.text: Three meals a day. That is more than a thousand decisions a year. And for a person with diabetes, every one hides the same question: does this fit my day?
Meet Maya and Daniel. They are made up, but you probably know them. They live in very different ways, and they run into the same wall.
Wrap and chips. Is that okay? I honestly don't know.
Maya has no time to plan. Her day is a car, a desk and a petrol station. So she guesses, or skips the meal, and worries all afternoon.
Most tools ask for a life with spare time.
Sunday. The whole week, planned.
Daniel is the opposite. He plans every meal for the week.
Wednesday. A late meeting. Pizza.
Then life happens. A plan that breaks feels like failing, and some people stop trying.
Two people. Two rhythms. What is missing is an answer that fits a real day.
Coffee with milk and a banana.
She types it the way she would say it. A few seconds later: it fits, and here is what is left of today.
Grilled chicken sandwich and an apple.
Not quite? It names a lighter swap, and counts that too.
Chicken salad instead. Fine.
Every number comes from a database, line by line. Open the receipt and check it yourself. A language model never makes one up.
In the diary, his plan stays on the page, dashed. Only what he really eats is counted.
Chicken fried rice.
A plan that broke is not a failure. It is just Wednesday.
How many units of insulin before pasta?
Some questions it will never answer. Doses belong to your care team, and it refuses before any model sees the question.
Grandma's cholent.
And when it does not know a dish, it says so, and calls the count an estimate.
A quick check on the go. A diary for the days a plan does not survive. One tool for both. Free to try at diabite.pro. A reference tool, not medical advice.
